title: Molecular Basis of Inheritance
description: Grade 12 Biology: DNA as the genetic material, its double-helix structure and replication, the central dogma with transcription and translation, and the genetic code.

topics.title: DNA: The Genetic Material and Its Structure
topics.concept:
Mendel's "factors" that carry traits are now known to be made of a molecule called DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid). DNA is the genetic material in almost all living things — it stores the instructions to build and run the organism and passes them from parents to offspring. (In a few viruses the genetic material is RNA.)

DNA is a long polymer of units called nucleotides. Each nucleotide has three parts: a nitrogenous base, a deoxyribose sugar and a phosphate group. There are four bases: adenine (A), thymine (T), guanine (G) and cytosine (C).

Watson and Crick (1953) worked out that DNA is a double helix — two strands twisted around each other like a spiral staircase. Key features:

  • The two strands run in opposite directions (antiparallel) and are held together by the bases pairing in the middle.
  • The base pairing is specific: A always pairs with T, and G always pairs with C (joined by hydrogen bonds). This is complementary base pairing.
  • Because of this rule, the two strands are complementary: knowing the order of bases on one strand tells you the order on the other.

This neat structure explains how DNA can store information (in the sequence of bases) and how it can be copied accurately.

examples.problem: Example 1: What are the three parts of a DNA nucleotide?
examples.solution:
Each unit has three components.

  • A nitrogenous base, a deoxyribose sugar and a phosphate group.
examples.answer: A nitrogenous base, a deoxyribose sugar and a phosphate group.

examples.problem: Example 2: State the base-pairing rule in DNA.
examples.solution:
Bases pair specifically.

  • A pairs with T; G pairs with C.
examples.answer: Adenine pairs with thymine (A–T) and guanine pairs with cytosine (G–C).

examples.problem: Example 3: If one DNA strand reads A-T-G-C, what is the sequence of the complementary strand?
examples.solution:
Apply the pairing rule to each base.

  • A→T, T→A, G→C, C→G.

recap:
• DNA = genetic material (RNA in some viruses); polymer of nucleotides (base + deoxyribose + phosphate).
  • Bases: A, T, G, C; Watson & Crick → double helix, antiparallel strands.
  • Complementary pairing: A–T, G–C (hydrogen bonds); the two strands are complementary.

quiz.q: In DNA, adenine always pairs with:
quiz.explanation: A pairs with T (and G with C) in DNA.

quiz.q: The double-helix structure of DNA was proposed by:
quiz.explanation: Watson and Crick proposed the DNA double helix in 1953.

topics.title: DNA Replication and the Central Dogma
topics.concept:
Before a cell divides, its DNA must be copied so each daughter cell gets a full set of instructions. This copying is DNA replication. The double helix "unzips" as the two strands separate, and each old strand acts as a template on which a new complementary strand is built (following A–T, G–C pairing), with the help of the enzyme DNA polymerase. The result is two identical DNA molecules, each having one old strand and one new strand. Because half of each new molecule is conserved from the parent, replication is called semi-conservative.

How does DNA actually control the cell? Through the central dogma of molecular biology, the flow of genetic information:

DNA → RNA → Protein

  • Transcription — the information in a gene (a stretch of DNA) is copied into a molecule of messenger RNA (mRNA). RNA is single-stranded, has ribose sugar, and uses the base uracil (U) in place of thymine.
  • Translation — the mRNA carries the message to the ribosomes, where it is "read" to join amino acids in the correct order to build a protein.

So genes work by directing the making of proteins, and proteins carry out the cell's functions and build its structures. This is how the information stored in DNA is finally turned into the features of the organism.

examples.problem: Example 1: Why is DNA replication called semi-conservative?
examples.solution:
Each new molecule keeps one old strand.

  • Each new DNA molecule has one old (parent) strand and one newly made strand.
  • So half of the original is conserved.
examples.answer: Because each new DNA molecule keeps one old strand and one new strand — half the original is conserved.

examples.problem: Example 2: State the central dogma of molecular biology.
examples.solution:
It is the flow of information.

  • DNA → RNA → Protein.
examples.answer: DNA → RNA → Protein (information flows from DNA to RNA to protein).

examples.problem: Example 3: What is the difference between transcription and translation?
examples.solution:
They are two different steps.

  • Transcription: DNA → mRNA (copying the gene into RNA).
  • Translation: mRNA → protein (reading RNA to build a protein at the ribosome).
examples.answer: Transcription makes mRNA from DNA; translation reads the mRNA to build a protein at the ribosome.

recap:
• Replication: DNA unzips, each strand is a template, new strands built by DNA polymerase; semi-conservative (one old + one new strand each).
  • Central dogma: DNA → RNA → Protein.
  • Transcription: DNA → mRNA (RNA: single-stranded, ribose, uracil for thymine).
  • Translation: mRNA read at ribosomes → protein.

quiz.q: DNA replication is described as semi-conservative because each new molecule has:
options: One old and one new strand
quiz.explanation: Each daughter molecule keeps one parental strand and one new strand.

quiz.q: The flow of information in the central dogma is:
quiz.explanation: The central dogma is DNA → RNA → Protein.

topics.title: The Genetic Code and the Human Genome
topics.concept:
How does the four-letter language of DNA (A, T, G, C) specify the twenty kinds of amino acids in proteins? Through the genetic code. The bases are read in groups of three, and each triplet of bases on the mRNA is called a codon. Each codon stands for one amino acid — for example, the codon AUG codes for the amino acid methionine and also acts as the "start" signal. A few codons are "stop" signals that end the protein.

Important features of the genetic code:

  • It is a triplet code (three bases per codon).
  • It is universal — almost the same in all organisms, from bacteria to humans, which is strong evidence that all life shares a common origin.
  • It is degenerate — most amino acids are coded by more than one codon.
  • It is non-overlapping and read in a fixed direction.

A gene is a segment of DNA that carries the code for one protein (or RNA). A change in the DNA sequence is a mutation; mutations create variation, and some cause disease (for example, a single base change causes sickle-cell anaemia).

The complete set of an organism's DNA is its genome. The Human Genome Project (completed 2003) mapped the entire human genome — about 3 billion base pairs and some 20,000–25,000 genes. Such knowledge, and tools like DNA fingerprinting (which uses unique patterns in a person's DNA), are now used in medicine, forensics (solving crimes, identifying people) and the study of evolution.

examples.solution:
The code is read in threes.

  • A codon is a triplet of three bases on the mRNA.
  • Each codon codes for one amino acid.
examples.answer: A codon is a group of three bases on mRNA that codes for one amino acid.

examples.problem: Example 2: What does it mean that the genetic code is 'universal'?
examples.solution:
It is shared across life.

  • The same codons stand for the same amino acids in almost all organisms.
  • This suggests a common origin of life.
examples.answer: Almost all organisms use the same codons for the same amino acids — evidence of a common origin of life.

examples.problem: Example 3: What is a mutation, and give an example of a disease it causes.
examples.solution:
A mutation changes the DNA sequence.

  • A mutation is a change in the DNA sequence.
  • A single base change causes sickle-cell anaemia.
examples.answer: A mutation is a change in the DNA sequence; for example, a single base change causes sickle-cell anaemia.

recap:
• Genetic code: bases read in threes (codons); each codon = one amino acid (AUG = start/methionine; stop codons end it).
  • Code is triplet, universal, degenerate, non-overlapping.
  • Gene = DNA segment coding a protein; mutation = change in sequence (e.g. sickle-cell anaemia).
  • Genome = all the DNA; Human Genome Project (~3 billion bp, ~20-25k genes); DNA fingerprinting in forensics/medicine.

quiz.q: A triplet of three bases that codes for one amino acid is a:
quiz.explanation: A codon is three bases coding for one amino acid.

quiz.q: A change in the DNA base sequence is called a:
quiz.explanation: A mutation is a change in the DNA sequence.

topics.title: Discovery of DNA as the Genetic Material and Gene Regulation
topics.concept:
How did scientists prove that DNA (and not protein) is the genetic material? Through a series of classic experiments:

  • Griffith's experiment — working with Streptococcus pneumoniae bacteria, Griffith found that a harmless strain could be made deadly by something passed from heat-killed virulent bacteria. He called it the "transforming principle" (the process is transformation), though he did not know it was DNA.
  • Avery, MacLeod and McCarty — they purified the transforming principle and showed it was DNA, because destroying DNA (not protein) stopped transformation.
  • Hershey and Chase — using bacteriophages (viruses that infect bacteria) with radioactively labelled DNA and protein, they showed that only the DNA entered the bacteria, finally confirming DNA as the genetic material.

Studying DNA's chemistry, Chargaff's rule states that in any DNA the amount of adenine equals thymine (A = T) and guanine equals cytosine (G = C). This base-pairing equivalence supported the Watson–Crick double-helix model.

Genes are not all switched on all the time; their activity is controlled by gene regulation. In bacteria this is explained by the operon concept — a group of genes controlled together by a switch. The classic example is the lac operon of E. coli (described by Jacob and Monod): the genes that digest lactose are normally switched off, and are turned on only when lactose is present. This lets the cell make the digesting enzymes only when they are needed, saving energy.

examples.solution:
It showed transformation.

  • A harmless strain became virulent due to a 'transforming principle' from heat-killed bacteria.
  • This hinted that genetic material can be transferred.
examples.answer: Griffith showed that a harmless bacterial strain could be transformed into a virulent one by a 'transforming principle' (later shown to be DNA).

examples.solution:
Base amounts are paired.

  • In DNA, A = T and G = C in amount.
examples.answer: In any DNA, the amount of adenine equals thymine (A = T) and guanine equals cytosine (G = C).

examples.problem: Example 3: When is the lac operon of E. coli switched on?
examples.solution:
It responds to lactose.

  • The lactose-digesting genes are normally off.
  • They are switched on only when lactose is present.
examples.answer: The lac operon is switched on only when lactose is present, so the enzymes are made only when needed.

recap:
• DNA proven as genetic material: Griffith (transformation), Avery–MacLeod–McCarty (it is DNA), Hershey–Chase (bacteriophage confirmation).
  • Chargaff's rule: A = T and G = C in amount.
  • Gene regulation via the operon; the lac operon of E. coli is switched on only when lactose is present.

quiz.q: The Hershey-Chase experiment used bacteriophages to prove that the genetic material is:
quiz.explanation: Only the labelled DNA entered the bacteria, confirming DNA as the genetic material.

quiz.q: According to Chargaff's rule, in DNA the amount of adenine equals that of:
quiz.explanation: A = T (and G = C) in amount — Chargaff's rule.

questions.q: The genetic material in almost all living organisms is:
questions.explanation: DNA is the genetic material (RNA in some viruses).

questions.q: The building blocks (monomers) of DNA are:
questions.explanation: DNA is a polymer of nucleotides.

questions.q: Which sugar is present in DNA?
questions.explanation: DNA contains deoxyribose sugar.

questions.q: In DNA, guanine pairs with:
questions.explanation: G pairs with C (and A with T).

questions.q: The double-helix model of DNA was proposed by:
questions.explanation: Watson and Crick proposed the double helix in 1953.

questions.q: Copying of DNA before cell division is called:
questions.explanation: DNA replication copies the DNA.

questions.q: DNA replication is:
questions.explanation: Each new molecule keeps one old strand — semi-conservative.

questions.q: The enzyme that builds new DNA strands is:
questions.explanation: DNA polymerase synthesises the new strand.

questions.q: The central dogma is:
questions.explanation: Information flows DNA → RNA → Protein.

questions.q: Copying a gene from DNA into mRNA is:
questions.explanation: Transcription makes mRNA from DNA.

questions.q: In RNA, the base that replaces thymine is:
questions.explanation: RNA uses uracil in place of thymine.

questions.q: Proteins are built from mRNA at the:
questions.explanation: Translation builds proteins at the ribosomes.

questions.q: A triplet of bases coding for one amino acid is a:
questions.explanation: A codon is three bases coding one amino acid.

questions.q: The genetic code being nearly the same in all organisms means it is:
questions.explanation: The code is universal, evidence of common ancestry.

questions.q: The complete set of an organism's DNA is its:
questions.explanation: The genome is all of an organism's DNA.

questions.q: The 'transforming principle' was first observed in the experiment of:
questions.explanation: Griffith observed transformation in Streptococcus pneumoniae.

questions.q: The lac operon of E. coli is switched on in the presence of:
questions.explanation: Lactose induces the lac operon, turning on the digesting genes.

questions.q: If one DNA strand reads 5'-AATGC-3', the complementary strand reads:
questions.explanation: Pairing A–T and G–C gives T-T-A-C-G as the complement.

questions.q: Complementary base pairing is the key to accurate replication because each old strand:
options: Specifies the exact sequence of its new partner
questions.explanation: Because A only pairs with T and G with C, each template dictates an exact complementary copy.

questions.q: A single base change in the DNA can alter one amino acid in a protein, as in sickle-cell anaemia. This shows that:
options: The base sequence of a gene determines the protein
questions.explanation: Changing the code changes the amino acid sequence, hence the protein — the basis of the disease.

questions.q: The genetic code is described as 'degenerate' because:
options: Most amino acids are coded by more than one codon
Each codon codes many amino acids
questions.explanation: Degeneracy means several different codons can specify the same amino acid.

questions.q: DNA fingerprinting can identify individuals because each person (except identical twins) has a:
questions.explanation: Variations in DNA make each person's profile unique, useful in forensics and identification.

questions.q: The near-universality of the genetic code across bacteria, plants and humans is strong evidence that all life:
questions.explanation: A shared code points to descent from a common ancestor.

questions.q: The lac operon staying OFF when no lactose is present benefits the cell by:
options: Saving energy by not making unneeded enzymes
questions.explanation: Producing lactose-digesting enzymes only when lactose is available avoids wasting resources.
